identity.title: Localized LLQ tenderness (with prior diverticulitis episode history)

technique.how: Palpate all four quadrants, leaving the painful area until last; record whether direct tenderness is confined to the left lower quadrant (versus diffuse or elsewhere), and whether there is guarding, rebound or a palpable mass. Ask specifically about previous confirmed episodes of diverticulitis and about vomiting.
technique.prerequisites: Patient supine and relaxed; analgesia does not preclude examination.

interpretation.positive_finding: Tenderness confined to the LLQ, especially with a prior episode, no vomiting and CRP >50 mg/L, makes acute diverticulitis very likely (PPV 97% for the three-feature rule in clinically suspected patients), and can allow treatment without imaging in uncomplicated cases in some pathways.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of isolated LLQ tenderness does not exclude diverticulitis (the three-feature rule captured only about one-third of confirmed cases); clinicians' overall clinical diagnosis has a sensitivity of roughly 0.64 with a high false-positive rate, so imaging (CT) is needed when features are incomplete.
interpretation.pitfalls: Redundant sigmoid, right-sided diverticulitis (more common in Asian patients) and elderly or immunosuppressed patients give atypical locations or minimal tenderness. Diffuse tenderness, rigidity or peritonism signals perforation or abscess, not uncomplicated diverticulitis.
interpretation.changes_what: Isolated LLQ tenderness + no vomiting + CRP>50: diverticulitis likely; consider CT to stage. Diffuse tenderness/peritonism or incomplete features: CT to exclude perforation, abscess or alternatives.

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: direct tenderness only in the LLQ AND absence of vomiting AND CRP >50 mg/L (Lameris rule, all three present) for final diagnosis of acute diverticulitis
estimates.population: 126 ED patients with acute abdominal pain and clinically suspected diverticulitis before imaging (80 with final diagnosis of diverticulitis), from a prospective cohort of 1,021 ED abdominal-pain patients, Netherlands
estimates.reference_standard: Final diagnosis by expert panel after imaging and follow-up
estimates.computed_from: 2x2 reconstructed from abstract among 126 suspected patients: 30 had all 3 features, 29 of whom had diverticulitis (TP 29, FP 1); 80 had diverticulitis in total (FN 51); 46 did not (TN 45). Sens 29/80 = 0.363; spec 45/46 = 0.978; LR+ 16.7; LR- 0.65; prevalence 80/126 = 0.635
estimates.quote: 30 patients had all 3 features (24%), of whom 29 had a final diagnosis of acute diverticulitis (97%; 95% CI: 83%-99%)

estimates.target_condition: Clinician's primary (admission) diagnosis of acute diverticulitis - overall clinical gestalt including LLQ tenderness, NOT the isolated sign
estimates.population: 3,349 patients admitted with abdominal pain of up to 7 days' duration, prospectively registered, Swedish hospital (145 with final diagnosis of diverticulitis)
estimates.quote: Sensitivity of diverticulitis as primary diagnosis was 64% and specificity 97%.

sources.citation: Laméris W, van Randen A, van Gulik TM et al. A clinical decision rule to establish the diagnosis of acute diverticulitis at the emergency department. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2010.

Laurell H, Hansson LE, Gunnarsson U. Acute diverticulitis--clinical presentation and differential diagnostics. Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland. 2007.

Toorenvliet BR, Bakker RF, Breslau PJ et al. Colonic diverticulitis: a prospective analysis of diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making. Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland. 2010.
Andeweg CS, Knobben L, Hendriks JC et al. How to diagnose acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis: proposal for a clinical scoring system. Annals of surgery. 2011.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a benign LLQ exam in immunosuppressed, steroid-treated or very elderly patients, in whom perforation can present with minimal tenderness.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Diffuse peritonism, rigidity, hypotension or a tender mass suggests perforation or abscess: urgent CT and surgical review.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No interobserver data for localised LLQ tenderness located.

extraction_notes: No study reporting sensitivity/specificity or LR for isolated LLQ tenderness as a single sign was found (searches: 'left lower quadrant tenderness diverticulitis likelihood ratio', 'diverticulitis clinical diagnosis prospective emergency department tenderness accuracy', Andeweg scoring). Hence status partially_quantified and both estimates are labelled as composite or gestalt, not the sign itself. Lameris 2010 (PMID 20485003): per-feature accuracy is in the paper's tables, which are not accessible (no PMC full text); the composite 2x2 was reconstructed from abstract counts. Note the abstract also states 'Of the 96 patients without all 3 features, 45 (47%) did not have diverticulitis' (Abstract, Results), consistent with TN 45. Toorenvliet 2010 (PMID 19183330; 802 consecutive ED abdominal-pain patients, 57 diverticulitis): 'The positive and negative predictive values for the clinical diagnosis of colonic diverticulitis were 0.65 and 0.98' (Abstract, Results); no sens/spec, so not entered. Andeweg 2011 (PMID 21346548; 287 CT-imaged ED patients, 43% ALCD): 'localization of abdominal tenderness in the lower left abdomen' and '1 or more previous episodes' were independent predictors (Abstract, Results) but no accuracy figures; supports adding prior-episode history to the finding. Prior-episode history in the id title has no stand-alone accuracy data.
